41660:
Joel gives no king's name and no date. That silence is part of the puzzle. The book mentions elders and priests but no king, a working temple, a city wall, Greeks buying Judean slaves from Phoenicians, and enemies (Tyre, Sidon, Philistia, Egypt, Edom) who fit several periods. It also quotes or echoes many other prophets: 'the Day of the LORD is near' (Obadiah, Zephaniah, Isaiah), 'beat your plowshares into swords' (reversing Isaiah and Micah), and 'the LORD roars from Zion' (Amos 1:2). For these reasons most scholars today place Joel in the Persian period, around 450-350 BC, after the temple was rebuilt. An older view dates it under the boy-king Joash (c. 835 BC), when priests ruled for him, which would explain the absence of a king; others suggest the late 600s BC. The date matters less for the message than for the question of who is quoting whom.

Locust plagues were a real and terrifying event in the ancient Near East and still are: desert locusts can travel in swarms of billions, eating every green thing and leaving famine behind. Joel describes waves of insects (named by four Hebrew words, perhaps stages of growth or kinds of locust) and a drought that dries up the streams. With no grain or wine, the daily grain and drink offerings at the temple had to stop, which was a spiritual crisis as much as an economic one (Joel 1:9; Joel 1:13).

The book moves from that local disaster to a cosmic one. In chapter 2 the locusts look like an invading army, and the 'Day of the LORD' becomes a day when God himself leads the army. Then the tone turns: if the people return, God will restore the land, pour out his Spirit, and judge the nations who scattered his people.
41662: A day when God acts decisively to judge and to save. Israel expected it to be good news against enemies; prophets like Joel warned it could fall on God's own people first, then on the nations.
41664: In a crisis a trumpet (shofar) summoned everyone, from elders to nursing babies and newlyweds, to fast, weep and pray at the temple. Repentance was communal, not private.
41666: Tearing clothes was the normal outward sign of grief. Joel does not abolish it but asks for the inward reality it was meant to express.
41668: Joel quotes God's self-description from Sinai, 'gracious and merciful, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love', a refrain that runs through the Twelve.
41670: 'Jehoshaphat' means 'the LORD judges'. The valley is a symbolic courtroom where nations are tried for scattering Israel and selling its children; later tradition placed it in the Kidron Valley.
41672: In Israel the Spirit came mostly on leaders and prophets. Joel promises the Spirit to sons and daughters, old and young, even slaves, fulfilling Moses' wish that all the LORD's people were prophets.
41673:
Joel is heard in the season of the High Holy Days. In many Ashkenazi communities Joel 2:15-27 ('Blow the shofar in Zion, sanctify a fast') is added to the haftarah of Shabbat Shuvah, joining Hosea 14 in calling Israel to return before Yom Kippur. The shofar, the fast, the gathering of every age group and the priests weeping 'between the porch and the altar' map directly onto the liturgy of the Days of Awe. Joel 2:13, 'rend your hearts and not your garments, and return to the LORD your God, for he is gracious and merciful', sums up the Jewish understanding of teshuvah: outward acts matter, but God wants the turned heart, and his mercy is the ground of hope.

Note that the Hebrew Bible divides Joel into four chapters: the English Joel 2:28-32 is Hebrew Joel 3, and English Joel 3 is Hebrew Joel 4. In Jewish reading the outpouring of the Spirit is a promise for the whole people of Israel in the messianic age; the rabbis connected it with the end of the long silence of prophecy and with Moses' wish in Numbers 11. The book's closing scenes, judgment of the nations for 'scattering my people Israel and dividing up my land' and the LORD dwelling in Zion, were read as assurances to a small, battered community that God had not forgotten his covenant with them.
41675: Wave after wave of insects and drought ruin vines, figs and grain; drinkers, farmers and priests are all called to mourn.
41677: Priests are told to proclaim a fast and gather everyone at the temple, because the Day of the LORD is near.
41679: The locust swarm becomes an army at the city walls, led by God himself; darkness covers the sky.
41681: 'Even now' God invites his people back, citing his gracious character; perhaps he will relent.
41683: God answers with pity: rain, harvest and repayment for the years the locusts ate.
41685: Afterward God pours out his Spirit on all kinds of people; signs in the sky precede the Day, and all who call on his name are saved.
41687: The nations are tried in the valley of decision; Judah is protected, the land flows with wine and water, and the LORD dwells in Zion.
41688: Joel: the Day of the LORD
41705: The time when God steps in to judge evil and rescue his people; 'great and very terrible', yet a refuge for those who call on him.
41706: To turn back to God; Joel pairs it with God's own 'turning' or relenting from disaster.
41707: Breath, wind, spirit: God's life-giving presence and power, which Joel promises to pour out like rain on everyone.
41709: To change course out of compassion; God 'relents over disaster' when people return.
41710: The locusts recall the eighth plague on Egypt; now Israel itself is struck, and the Sinai creed of God's mercy is the way back.
41711: Joel ends with 'the LORD roars from Zion' and the mountains dripping sweet wine; Amos opens and closes with the same lines, stitching the two books together in the Twelve.
41712: Joel reverses the famous peace oracle: 'beat your plowshares into swords' turns Micah's and Isaiah's words around for the final battle.
41713: Peter interprets the Spirit's coming at Pentecost as Joel's prophecy, adding 'in the last days'.
41714: Paul quotes 'everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved' to show there is no distinction between Jew and Greek.
41715: Revelation's locust-army, darkened sun and harvest of the nations draw on Joel's imagery.
41716: The New Testament reads Joel as a map for the age that begins with Jesus. Peter says the Spirit poured out at Pentecost is what Joel spoke of, because the risen and exalted Jesus has received the Spirit and poured it out (Acts 2:16-21; Acts 2:33). The 'name of the LORD' on which people call is applied to Jesus himself (Acts 2:21; Acts 2:36; Rom 10:9-13), a striking move for Jewish writers. Jesus' own warnings about sun and moon darkening before the coming of the Son of Man echo Joel's signs (Mark 13:24-26). Jewish interpreters read the same promises as still awaiting the messianic age for Israel, with the outpouring of the Spirit and the gathering to Zion yet to come in full. Christians also tend to see a 'now and not yet': the Spirit has come, but the final Day and the full judgment of the nations remain ahead.
41718: Many evangelicals know Joel almost entirely through Acts 2: Joel is 'the Pentecost prophet', and chapters 1 and 3 are background noise.
41719: Joel's promise of the Spirit grows out of a story: a ruined land, a nation that fasts and returns, and a God who restores harvests and then pours his Spirit on everyone, including slaves. It is about the renewal of the covenant people and their land, and it ends with justice for the victims of war and slavery (Joel 3:3-6). Scholars such as James Crenshaw and Hans Walter Wolff stress this communal and land-centred setting; Jewish readers hear it as a promise to Israel.
41720: Evangelical scholars (e.g. Leslie Allen, Craig Keener in his Acts commentary) answer that Peter is not ignoring context but claiming that the 'last days' of Joel have begun with Jesus, and that Luke deliberately extends Joel's 'all flesh' to include Gentiles. Keener also notes Peter quotes enough of Joel to point hearers to the whole passage, a common Jewish practice. So Pentecost is a legitimate fulfilment; the problem is only when the rest of Joel is forgotten.
41721: Keeping the whole of Joel means the Spirit is linked to repentance, justice and the restoration of creation, not only to private spiritual experience or speaking in tongues.
41722: 'I will restore the years the locust has eaten' (Joel 2:25)
41723: This verse is widely used as a personal promise that God will give back lost time, wasted years, money or relationships to an individual believer.
41724: The promise was spoken to a community that had fasted and returned to God after a literal agricultural disaster. 'The years' are failed harvests; restoration is rain, full threshing floors and food for the whole people, so that they will 'know that I am in the midst of Israel' (Joel 2:27).
41725: Pastoral writers point out that the verse reveals God's character as restorer, and applying that character to personal loss is a natural extension many careful preachers make. Most evangelical commentators (e.g. Allen, Stuart) accept a principle-level application while cautioning against treating it as a guaranteed refund of every personal loss.
41726: The richer reading roots hope in God's covenant faithfulness to a people and their land, and avoids promising individuals specific outcomes the text does not promise.
41727: For a small Judean community the book turned a natural disaster into a call to return together to God, and gave assurance that God still lived in Zion and would one day judge the empires that had scattered and enslaved them.
41728: Joel shows a whole community responding to crisis with honest lament and shared repentance. It holds together disaster, mercy and the Spirit, and insists that God's gifts are for 'all flesh': young and old, women and men, slaves and free.
41729: A shepherd from Judah tells prosperous Israel that its religion is worthless while it crushes the poor, because the God who chose them holds them most responsible.
41730: A Judean from Tekoa, a village on the edge of the wilderness south of Bethlehem. He calls himself a herdsman (noqed, a word also used of a sheep-breeder in 2 Kgs 3:4) and a tender of sycamore figs, and denies being a professional prophet or a 'son of a prophet'. He was sent north to preach in Israel.
41731: The heading (Amos 1:1) and his clash with the priest Amaziah at Bethel (Amos 7:10-15). Scholars accept the core oracles as his; debate centres on a few passages that may come from later editors.
41732: Bethel and Samaria (spoken); Tekoa and Judah (written down)
41733: Amos preached at the northern royal shrine of Bethel and in Samaria. After being expelled he probably returned south, where his words were collected.
41734: The northern kingdom of Israel, especially its wealthy elite
41736: Under Jeroboam II Israel had recovered lost territory and grown rich. Ivory-inlaid houses, winter and summer homes and lavish feasts sat alongside debt slavery, rigged courts and dishonest markets, while the shrines were crowded with worshippers.
41737: 'Two years before the earthquake' (Amos 1:1), probably in the 760s or early 750s BC.
41738: Jeroboam II becomes king of Israel (approximate); his long reign restores Israel's borders (2 Kgs 14:25).
41739: A total solar eclipse is recorded in Assyrian sources (15 June 763 BC), possibly echoed in Amos 8:9.
41740: A major earthquake in the Levant, remembered centuries later (Zech 14:5) and visible in destruction layers at sites such as Hazor.
41741: Tiglath-pileser III revives Assyria, which will soon fulfil Amos's warnings of exile.
41742:
Amos spoke in a short window of peace. Assyria was weak for a few decades in the early 700s BC, and Damascus had been crushed, so Israel under Jeroboam II expanded to its old borders. The capital, Samaria, flourished: excavators found carved ivory panels there that once decorated furniture, a vivid match for Amos's 'beds of ivory' (Amos 6:4) and 'houses of ivory' (Amos 3:15). Ostraca (inscribed potsherds) from Samaria record shipments of wine and oil to the capital, showing how produce flowed from the countryside to the elite.

That wealth came at a price. Small farmers who had a bad year borrowed against their land or even sold themselves into debt slavery; creditors seized cloaks taken as pledges and used them at feasts in shrines (Amos 2:8). Merchants used small measures and heavy weights (Amos 8:5). Judges at the city gate took bribes (Amos 5:12). Meanwhile worship flourished at Bethel, Gilgal and Beersheba, with tithes, freewill offerings and loud songs.

Amos was an outsider from Judah, preaching at the king's own sanctuary. The priest Amaziah reported him to Jeroboam for conspiracy and told him to go home (Amos 7:10-13). His book ends with the hope of David's fallen 'booth' raised again, which many scholars think was added after the fall of Jerusalem, though others argue Amos himself held out such hope.
41743: Amos begins by condemning Israel's neighbours for war crimes ('for three transgressions and for four'), drawing applause from his audience, and then springs the trap: the eighth and climactic nation judged is Israel itself.
41745: Israel assumed that being chosen meant protection. Amos turns it around: 'You only have I known... therefore I will punish you.' Privilege raises accountability.
41747: The city gate was the local courtroom where elders heard cases. 'Hate evil, love good, establish justice in the gate' means fixing the legal system, not just personal kindness.
41749: Justice (mishpat) and righteousness (tsedaqah) together describe a society where the weak get a fair hearing and right relationships are restored. Amos wants them to roll like a never-failing stream.
41751: A marzeah was an exclusive banqueting club known from other ancient texts, with drinking and reclining. Amos mocks Samaria's elite lounging at such feasts while the nation collapses.
41753: Israel longed for the Day of the LORD as victory over enemies. Amos is the earliest prophet to say it will be darkness, not light, for Israel.
41754:
In the Jewish reading cycle Amos 2:6-3:8 is the haftarah for parashat Vayeshev, where Joseph is sold by his brothers: Amos's charge that Israel 'sold the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals' (Amos 2:6) was linked by the rabbis to the sale of Joseph. Amos 9:7-15 is read (in Ashkenazi practice) with Acharei Mot, setting Amos's picture of a restored Israel alongside the Day of Atonement laws. The Talmud (*Makkot* 24a) famously says that the 613 commandments were summed up by David in eleven principles, by Isaiah in six, by Micah in three, and by Amos in one: 'Seek me and live' (Amos 5:4).

For Jewish readers Amos is not an attack on ritual as such; the same Torah commanded sacrifices and festivals. It is a covenant reminder that the God who brought Israel out of Egypt also commanded care for the widow, the orphan, the stranger and the debtor (Exod 22:21-27; Deut 24:10-15). Worship without that justice is noise. Abraham Joshua Heschel's description of the prophets as people who felt God's pathos, his deep emotional involvement with human injustice, drew heavily on Amos and shaped modern Jewish social ethics, including Heschel's own march with Martin Luther King Jr., who quoted Amos 5:24.
41756: A thunderous opening: God's voice from Jerusalem withers even Carmel.
41758: Seven neighbours are condemned for cruelty; then Israel is condemned for selling the poor, sexual abuse and exploitation in worship.
41760: Rhetorical questions build to the point: God has spoken, so the prophet must speak; luxury and false worship will be torn down.
41762: A funeral song for Israel, a call to seek God and justice, and a rejection of festivals without righteousness.
41764: The comfortable elite of Samaria will go first into exile.
41766: Locusts, fire, plumb line, summer fruit and the altar struck; Amos is expelled from Bethel by Amaziah.
41768: After judgment, God will raise David's fallen shelter, restore the people and plant them in their land for good.
41788: Fair judgment and the restoring of right order, especially for the vulnerable; Amos complains Israel has turned it into poison.
41789: Right relationships within the covenant community, shown in how the weak are treated.
41790: To seek out, inquire of, turn to; seeking God is set against seeking shrines.
41791: Those left after judgment; Amos makes it a sobering image (two legs from a lion's mouth) but also a sliver of hope.
41792: Kings describes Jeroboam II's expansion and briefly notes his religion; Amos shows what that prosperity looked like on the ground.
41793: Amos's charges reflect Torah laws about pledges, fair weights, care for the poor and the stranger.
41794: Amos and Hosea preached to the same kingdom at nearly the same time: Amos stresses justice, Hosea loyal love.
41795: At the Jerusalem council James quotes Amos 9:11-12 (in its Greek form) to show that God always meant to include Gentiles in the rebuilt house of David.
41796: James' warnings to the rich who withhold wages and live in luxury are in the spirit of Amos.
41797: Zechariah remembers 'the earthquake in the days of Uzziah', the same quake that dates Amos.
41798: Jesus stands in Amos's line when he says that worship without reconciliation and justice is empty (Matt 5:23-24) and when he warns the rich and comfortable (Luke 6:24-25; Luke 16:19-31). The early church saw the raising of 'David's fallen booth' fulfilled in the risen Son of David, whose restored kingdom gathers 'all the nations called by my name' (Acts 15:16-17). Jewish interpreters read Amos 9:11 as the future restoration of the Davidic kingdom under the Messiah; the Talmud even refers to the Messiah as 'son of the fallen ones' (bar nafle) from this verse (*Sanhedrin* 96b). Both traditions see in Amos a God whose kingdom joins worship and justice.
41799: Amos as either 'only personal holiness' or 'only politics'
41800: Some evangelical preaching spiritualises Amos into a call to personal holiness and sincere worship, leaving out economics; some activist preaching turns Amos into a political programme and leaves out God and worship.
41801: Amos joins the two. Israel's sins are listed together: idolatry, sexual abuse, debt slavery, corrupt courts and cheating merchants (Amos 2:6-8; Amos 8:4-6). M. Daniel Carroll R. and Shalom Paul show that his targets are concrete social structures and that his standard is the covenant God gave at the exodus (Amos 2:10; Amos 3:1-2). For a collectivist society, sin and justice were communal, not only individual.
41802: Evangelical scholars such as Carroll R. and Gary Smith argue that Amos's justice is grounded in God's character and covenant, not in a modern ideology, and caution against directly mapping ancient Israel's theocratic laws onto modern state policy. They agree that both a purely private and a purely political reading flatten the book.
41803: Amos will not let worship and justice be separated: God rejects songs from people who exploit the poor, and he grounds justice in knowing him.
41804: 'Can two walk together unless they are agreed?' (Amos 3:3)
41805: The verse is often quoted as advice about marriage, friendship or church unity: do not partner with people who do not share your beliefs.
41806: It is the first of a chain of rhetorical questions about cause and effect (a lion roars because it has prey; a trap springs because something touched it). The chain leads to its point: disaster comes because God has acted, and a prophet speaks because God has spoken (Amos 3:6-8). It defends Amos's right to preach, not a principle of relationships.
41807: Few commentators of any school defend the relational reading as the meaning of the verse. Some preachers argue the principle (shared direction is needed for shared walking) is true elsewhere in Scripture (2 Cor 6:14), but evangelical commentators like Gary Smith and Billy Smith agree that Amos 3:3 itself is about prophetic authority.
41808: Read in context, the verse confronts listeners with a God who has spoken and must be heard, which is far more searching than a tip about choosing friends.
41809: Israel heard that its prosperity and full shrines were not proof of God's favour. Within forty years Assyria fulfilled Amos's warnings. Judeans who kept his words learned that the same standard applied to them.
41810: Amos challenges comfortable religious communities to ask who pays for their comfort, whether their courts and markets are fair, and whether their worship is matched by justice. It also warns against assuming that being God's people guarantees his approval.
41811: The Bible's shortest prophetic book condemns Edom for betraying its brother Judah on the day Jerusalem fell, and promises that the kingdom will finally belong to the LORD.
41813: Nothing is known of him beyond his name, which was common. Jewish tradition (Talmud *Sanhedrin* 39b) identifies him with Obadiah, Ahab's steward who hid a hundred prophets (1 Kgs 18:3-4), and makes him an Edomite convert, so that Edom is judged by one of its own. Modern scholars treat that as a homiletic tradition, not history.
41814: Only the one-word heading 'The vision of Obadiah' (Obad 1:1). His date is inferred from the events he describes.
41815: Judah, probably among those left in the land after 586 BC
41816: The vivid description of Edom at the gates of Jerusalem suggests an eyewitness or someone close to the event; some suggest Babylon, but there is no evidence for it.
41817: Grieving Judeans (addressed indirectly through an oracle against Edom)
41819: Jerusalem has been sacked. Edom, Judah's 'brother' nation descended from Esau, stood by, gloated, looted the city and handed fleeing survivors over to the enemy. The oracle assures the victims that God has seen.
41820: Edom revolts from Judah under Jehoram (2 Kgs 8:20-22), the setting proposed by the early-date view.
41821: Babylon takes Jerusalem and deports King Jehoiachin; ostraca from Arad in this period show the fortress expecting trouble from Edom.
41822: Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the temple; Edom's role is remembered bitterly (Ps 137:7; Lam 4:21-22).
41823: Nabonidus of Babylon campaigns against Edom, beginning its decline; Arab groups and later the Nabataeans move into its territory.
41824: John Hyrcanus conquers the Idumeans (Edom's descendants in southern Judea) and forces them to adopt Judaism (Josephus, *Antiquities* 13).
